unit-sci-phasechg.title: Chemistry · 2 Phase Changes
unit-sci-phasechg.srcName: Science update of 9/10 (teacher email) + the class Chemistry unit

summary.text: All six phase changes — melting, freezing, evaporation and boiling, condensation, sublimation and deposition — what each one starts and ends as, which way the energy travels, the temperatures where water changes, and why heating something sometimes changes its temperature and sometimes changes its phase instead.

why.text: The first chemistry quiz covers phases of matter AND phase changes, so this is the other half of what is being asked. It is also the part with the most vocabulary in it, and almost all of that vocabulary collapses into one rule once you see it: up the ladder takes energy in, down the ladder gives energy out.

objectives.text: Name all six phase changes and say which phase each one starts and ends in.
Say whether a given change takes energy in or gives energy off, using the direction it travels rather than memorising each one.
Tell evaporation from boiling, and condensation from evaporation.
Give the melting/freezing point and the boiling point of water in both Celsius and Fahrenheit.
Explain why an iced drink stays cold until the last ice melts.
Explain why mass does not change during a phase change.

parentNote.text: Built from the teacher’s Science update of 9/10, which names the first chemistry quiz (September 17) as covering "the phases of matter and the phase changes" — the Phases of Matter lesson shipped a day earlier covers the first half, and this covers the second. Three things are worth knowing about how it is built. First, every energy question is taught through ONE rule rather than six facts: up the solid-liquid-gas ladder always takes energy in, down always gives it off, so naming the direction answers the energy question with nothing extra to memorise. Second, evaporation-versus-condensation is the pair students swap most often, so it gets its own card with a hook (conDENSation moves towards the DENSer phase) as well as a question. Third, two traps get deliberate airtime because they are reasoning errors rather than vocabulary gaps: frost is deposition and not freezing (freezing starts from a liquid, and there was never liquid water on that windscreen), and "keeping the cold in" is backwards — cold is the absence of heat, so insulation slows heat moving IN. The teacher also notes that for quizzes she should study her highlighted notes and past homework sheets; this app is the extra practice on top of those, not a replacement for them.

nextUp.text: Get the six names cold first — what each one starts as and ends as. Then the energy half is free: up the ladder takes heat in, down gives it off.

cards.def:
**A phase change is matter switching between solid, liquid and gas.**
• The stuff itself does not change — ice, water and steam are all water.
• What changes is how much energy the particles have, and therefore how they are arranged and how fast they move.

**Melting is solid → liquid, and it needs energy IN.**
• Adding heat makes the particles vibrate harder until they break free of their fixed positions and start sliding past one another.
• An ice cube on a warm counter is melting because heat is moving INTO it.

**Freezing is liquid → solid, and it gives energy OUT.**
• The particles slow down until they lock into place.
• Freezing is melting run backwards, which is why they happen at the same temperature.

**Both are liquid → gas, and both need energy IN. The difference is where and when.**
• Evaporation happens only at the SURFACE, and at any temperature — a puddle dries up on a cool day.
• Boiling happens all the way THROUGH, and only once the liquid reaches its boiling point — that is what the bubbles from the bottom are.

**Condensation is gas → liquid, and it gives energy OUT.**
• The particles slow down enough to stick together into a liquid again.
• The water on the outside of a cold glass did not leak through it — it is water vapour from the air turning back into liquid on the cold surface.

**Sublimation is solid → gas, skipping liquid entirely, and it needs energy IN.**
• Dry ice is the famous one: it goes straight to a gas and leaves no puddle.
• Snow can slowly sublime away on a cold sunny day without ever melting.

**Deposition is gas → solid, skipping liquid, and it gives energy OUT.**
• Frost on a window forms this way — water vapour in the air becomes ice directly, without being liquid water first.
• It is sublimation run backwards.

cards.term: Energy in, or energy out — the one rule
cards.def:
**Moving UP the ladder (solid → liquid → gas) always takes energy IN. Moving DOWN always gives energy OUT.**
• In: melting, evaporation, boiling, sublimation.
• Out: freezing, condensation, deposition.
• Work out which direction the change goes and you already know the answer — there is nothing else to memorise.
cards.hint: Up the ladder costs you. Down the ladder pays you back.

cards.term: Melting point and freezing point are the same number
cards.def:
**For water, 0°C (32°F) — the one temperature where ice melts and water freezes.**
• They are two names for one boundary; which one happens depends on whether heat is going in or coming out.
• Different substances have different values — iron melts near 1,538°C.

**For water, 100°C (212°F) — the temperature at which a liquid boils all the way through.**
• Below it, water can still evaporate from its surface; it just cannot boil.
• Like the melting point, it belongs to the substance, not to water alone.

cards.term: It is the same stuff throughout
cards.def:
**A phase change rearranges particles. It never turns one substance into another.**
• Melt an ice cube and you get exactly the same water, in a different phase.
• Nothing is created and nothing is destroyed — a sealed jar of ice weighs the same once the ice has melted.

cards.term: Every phase change can run backwards
cards.def:
**Add energy and it goes one way; take energy away and it goes back.**
• Melt and freeze, evaporate and condense, sublime and deposit — three pairs, each the reverse of the other.
• So a puddle that dried up can come back as rain later. The water did not go anywhere.

cards.term: Evaporation or condensation? The commonest mix-up
cards.def:
**Evaporation makes a gas. Condensation makes a liquid.**
• The two words get swapped more often than any other pair in this unit.
• A hook: conDENSation makes something DENSer — gas is the least dense phase, liquid is denser, so the arrow points from gas to liquid.
cards.hint: Condense → denser → towards liquid. Evaporate → vapour → towards gas.

cards.term: Dew and frost are the same story at two temperatures
cards.def:
**Dew is condensation; frost is deposition.**
• On a cool night, water vapour in the air becomes liquid droplets on the grass — dew.
• On a night below freezing, that vapour becomes ice crystals directly, with no liquid step — frost.
• Both give energy out; only the destination differs.

**Sometimes heat makes something warmer; sometimes it changes its phase instead.**
• Heating ice below 0°C makes it warmer ice.
• Once it reaches 0°C, the heat goes into melting it rather than raising the temperature — which is why an iced drink stays cold until the last ice is gone.

**Melting, freezing, evaporation (and boiling), condensation, sublimation, deposition.**
• Four of them pass through liquid; two skip it.
• The two that skip liquid — sublimation and deposition — are the pair most often left off a list, so name them first when you are checking your work.

questions.q: What happens to a substance during a phase change?
opts: Its particles rearrange, but it is still the same substance
It turns into a completely different substance altogether
Some of its particles are destroyed and the rest survive
It gains extra new particles from the air all around it
questions.hint: Ice, water and steam — how many different substances is that?
steps: A phase change moves matter between solid, liquid and gas.
What changes is how much energy the particles have and how they are arranged.
The particles themselves are exactly the same ones as before.
So it rearranges without becoming anything new.

ex.main: **Ice, liquid water and steam are all water — a phase change rearranges particles rather than replacing them.** Nothing is created or destroyed either, which is why a sealed jar weighs the same before and after the ice in it melts.
ex.tip: Same stuff, new arrangement. That is the whole idea.

questions.q: A tray of water is left in the freezer overnight. What is this change called?
opts: Melting
Freezing
Condensation
Sublimation
questions.hint: Name the phase it starts in and the phase it ends in.
steps: The water starts as a liquid and ends as a solid.
Liquid to solid is freezing.
Melting is the reverse of that.
So the answer is freezing.

ex.main: **Liquid to solid is freezing.** Naming a change is always the same two steps: what phase did it start in, and what phase did it end in. Condensation ends as a liquid and sublimation ends as a gas, so neither fits.
ex.tip: Start phase, end phase, then name it. Never guess from the setting.

questions.q: Which pair of changes both need energy to be ADDED?
opts: Freezing and deposition
Freezing and condensation
Melting and evaporation
Condensation and deposition
questions.hint: Which direction on the solid-liquid-gas ladder does each one travel?
steps: Adding energy moves a substance UP the ladder: solid to liquid to gas.
Melting is solid to liquid and evaporation is liquid to gas — both are upward.
Freezing, condensation and deposition all move downward, so all three give energy off.
So the pair that takes energy in is melting and evaporation.

ex.main: **Up the ladder always takes energy in; down always gives energy out — and that single rule answers every question of this kind.** There is nothing to memorise per change: work out which direction it travels and the energy follows.
ex.tip: Solid → liquid → gas costs energy. The way back returns it.

questions.q: Water droplets appear on the outside of a cold glass of lemonade. Where did they come from?
opts: The glass melted slightly and the drips are glass
Lemonade seeped out through tiny holes in the glass
The cold made new water out of the air’s nitrogen
Water vapour in the air turned to liquid on the cold glass
questions.hint: Air has water in it, even when it does not look wet.
steps: The air around the glass carries invisible water vapour.
The cold glass cools that vapour down, slowing its particles.
Slowed enough, the vapour becomes liquid water on the surface — condensation.
Nothing came through the glass, and nothing new was created.

ex.main: **This is condensation: water vapour already in the air becomes liquid on the cold surface.** Glass has no holes for lemonade to escape through, and a phase change never makes water out of a different substance — the water was already there, just invisible.
ex.tip: If a cold thing gets wet on the outside, think condensation first.

questions.q: Dry ice is put on a table and slowly disappears, leaving no puddle behind. What is happening?
opts: It is going straight from solid to gas
It is melting, and the puddle dries too fast to see
It is condensing into the air
It is freezing even harder
questions.hint: What is missing that would be there if it had melted?
steps: A solid that melts leaves a liquid behind.
There is no liquid here at all.
So it must be going straight from solid to gas, skipping liquid — sublimation.
That is exactly what dry ice is known for.

ex.main: **Sublimation is solid straight to gas, with no liquid step — which is why there is no puddle.** The absence of the liquid is the whole clue. Condensation would produce a liquid, and freezing would make it more solid, not less.
ex.tip: No puddle means no liquid stage. That rules melting out immediately.

questions.q: Frost forms on a car windscreen overnight. Which change is that, and does it take heat in or give heat off?
opts: Condensation, and it gives heat off
Deposition, and it gives heat off
Sublimation, and it takes heat in
Freezing, and it takes heat in
questions.hint: Frost is ice. What was it immediately before it was ice — a liquid, or a gas?
steps: Frost forms from water vapour in the air, not from liquid water sitting on the glass.
Gas straight to solid, skipping liquid, is deposition.
That is a move DOWN the ladder, so it gives heat off.
Freezing would be right if liquid water had been there first, but it was not.

ex.main: **Frost is deposition: water vapour becomes ice directly, and going down the ladder always gives heat off.** The tempting answer is freezing — but freezing starts from a liquid, and dry glass on a cold night has vapour on it, not water. Dew is the version that stops at liquid.
ex.tip: Dew stops at liquid. Frost goes all the way to solid in one step.

questions.q: A puddle dries up completely on a cool, breezy day — nowhere near 100°C. How is that possible?
opts: The water soaked into the air as a liquid
The puddle must have reached its boiling point somehow
Evaporation happens at the surface, at any temperature
Cool air destroys water
questions.hint: What is the difference between evaporating and boiling?
steps: Boiling happens all the way through a liquid, and only at its boiling point.
Evaporation happens only at the surface, and at any temperature.
A puddle has a large surface and plenty of time, so it can evaporate away entirely.
So it evaporated, without ever boiling.

ex.main: **Evaporation needs no particular temperature — it happens at the surface whenever particles there have enough energy to escape.** Boiling is the one that waits for a specific temperature and happens throughout. Water is never destroyed; it left as an invisible gas.
ex.tip: Bubbles from the bottom mean boiling. A puddle just quietly shrinking is evaporation.

questions.q: Which change is the exact reverse of melting?
opts: Deposition
Evaporation
Condensation
Freezing
questions.hint: Melting goes solid to liquid. Which change goes the other way along that same step?
steps: Melting is solid to liquid.
Its reverse must be liquid to solid.
That is freezing.
Condensation is gas to liquid, which is a different step of the ladder.

ex.main: **Freezing is melting run backwards — same two phases, opposite direction, which is why they happen at the same temperature.** The six changes come in three reverse pairs: melt/freeze, evaporate/condense, sublime/deposit.
ex.tip: Learn them in pairs and you have only three things to remember.

questions.q: Ice melts at 0°C. At what temperature does liquid water freeze?
opts: It depends on how much water there is
questions.hint: Freezing and melting are the same boundary crossed in opposite directions.
steps: Melting and freezing are reverses of each other.
They happen at the same temperature — the boundary between solid and liquid.
For water that boundary is 0°C.
So water freezes at 0°C, the same temperature at which ice melts.

ex.main: **The melting point and the freezing point are one temperature with two names — 0°C for water.** Which of the two actually happens depends on whether heat is going in or coming out. 32 is the same boundary in Fahrenheit, not in Celsius, and the amount of water makes no difference at all.
ex.tip: One boundary, two names. The direction of the heat decides which.

questions.q: An iced drink sits in a warm room. The ice slowly melts, but the drink stays cold the whole time until the last ice is gone. Why?
opts: Ice keeps making more cold and pushes it into the drink around it
The arriving heat goes into melting the ice, not warming the drink
The drink is already as cold as anything in the room can get
Warm air can only reach a solid, so the liquid stays untouched
questions.hint: Heat can do two different jobs. Which one is it doing while ice is still present?
steps: Heat arriving at something can either raise its temperature or drive a phase change.
While ice is still melting, the arriving heat is spent on the melting itself.
So the temperature stays put rather than climbing.
Once the last ice has melted, the heat has nothing to melt and the drink starts warming up.

ex.main: **Heat has two possible jobs, and while a phase change is underway it does that one instead of raising the temperature.** This is why ice keeps a drink cold so effectively, and why the drink warms up quickly the moment the ice is gone. Nothing "makes cold" — heat moves in, and the melting absorbs it.
ex.tip: Cold is not a thing that travels. Heat is.

questions.q: A sealed jar holds an ice cube and nothing else. The ice melts completely. What happens to the jar’s total mass?
opts: It goes up, because liquid is denser
It goes down, because ice is heavier
It stays exactly the same
It goes down, because water escapes
questions.hint: The jar is sealed. Did anything get in or out?
steps: A phase change rearranges particles; it does not create or destroy them.
The jar is sealed, so nothing left and nothing entered.
The same particles are inside, just arranged as a liquid instead of a solid.
So the total mass is unchanged.

ex.main: **Mass is conserved through every phase change — the same particles are still in the jar.** Liquid water IS denser than ice, which is why ice floats, but density is mass per space taken up: the water takes up slightly less room while weighing exactly the same.
ex.tip: Density changing and mass changing are two different claims.

questions.q: Which statement about evaporation and condensation is correct?
opts: Both produce a liquid, at different temperatures
Evaporation produces a liquid; condensation produces a gas
Both produce a gas, at different speeds
Evaporation produces a gas; condensation produces a liquid
questions.hint: One hook: which word sounds like it is making something denser?
steps: Evaporation turns a liquid into vapour — that is, into a gas.
Condensation turns a gas back into a liquid.
A gas is the least dense phase and a liquid is denser, so conDENSation points from gas towards liquid.
So evaporation makes a gas and condensation makes a liquid.

ex.main: **These two get swapped more than any other pair in the unit, so it is worth a hook: conDENSation moves towards the DENSer phase, the liquid.** They are exact reverses of each other, which also means one takes energy in and the other gives it off.
ex.tip: Evaporate → vapour → gas. That half names itself.

questions.q: Which two changes skip the liquid phase completely?
opts: Sublimation and deposition
Melting and freezing
Evaporation and condensation
Boiling and melting
questions.hint: Four of the six changes pass through liquid. Which two do not?
steps: Melting, freezing, evaporation and condensation all have liquid at one end.
Sublimation goes solid straight to gas.
Deposition goes gas straight to solid.
So those two are the pair that skips liquid.

ex.main: **Sublimation and deposition are the only two that jump between solid and gas directly.** They are also the two most often left off a list of the six, so naming them first is a good habit when checking your work — dry ice and frost are the everyday examples.
ex.tip: Four go through liquid. Two do not. Learn the two.

questions.q: What is the boiling point of water?
questions.hint: Two of these are the same temperature in different units — and only one is in Celsius.
steps: Water boils at 100°C.
That is the same temperature as 212°F, but the question asks in Celsius.
0°C is where water freezes and melts, not where it boils.
So the answer is 100°C.

ex.main: **Water boils at 100°C, which is 212°F.** Check the unit before you pick: 212 and 32 are the two Fahrenheit values in disguise, and 0°C is the melting-and-freezing boundary rather than the boiling one.
ex.tip: Water: 0 and 100 in Celsius, 32 and 212 in Fahrenheit.

questions.q: A cook wants an ice cube to melt faster. Which of these would actually help, and why?
opts: Wrap it in a towel, so the cold cannot escape
Put it somewhere colder, so it works harder
Put it somewhere warmer, so heat moves into it more quickly
Leave it sealed in the freezer, where it has more time
questions.hint: Melting needs something moving INTO the ice. What is it, and how do you supply more?
steps: Melting is a move up the ladder, so it needs heat going in.
The faster heat arrives, the faster it melts.
A warmer place delivers heat faster.
Colder places, insulation and the freezer all slow the heat down, so all three would make it slower.

ex.main: **Melting needs heat arriving, so anything that speeds the heat up speeds the melting up.** A towel is insulation — it slows heat moving in, which is exactly why a wrapped ice cube lasts longer. And nothing "keeps cold in": cold is the absence of heat, not a substance.
ex.tip: Ask what has to move, then ask what makes it move faster.

questions.q: Steam from a kettle hits a cool window and beads of water appear. Name the change, and say which way the heat went.
opts: Deposition, and heat entered the water
Condensation, and heat entered the water
Evaporation, and heat left the water
Condensation, and heat left the water
questions.hint: Gas to liquid is which change, and which direction on the ladder is that?
steps: The steam is a gas and the beads are a liquid.
Gas to liquid is condensation.
That is a move down the ladder.
Down the ladder gives heat off, so heat left the water and went into the window.

ex.main: **Condensation, and the heat went out of the water and into the cool window.** Both halves matter: naming the change is the first step, and the direction of travel then decides the energy without any extra memorising. Deposition would have made ice, not liquid beads.
ex.tip: Name it, then read the direction off the ladder.

questions.q: Put these in the order they happen as a block of ice in a pan is heated steadily from well below freezing.
opts: The ice warms up to 0°C
The ice melts into liquid water
The water warms up to 100°C
The water boils into steam
questions.hint: Heat does two different jobs, and they take turns.
steps: Heat first raises the temperature of the solid ice up to its melting point.
At 0°C the heat goes into melting instead, turning the ice into liquid water.
Once it is all liquid, the heat raises the temperature again, up to 100°C.
At 100°C the heat goes into boiling, turning the water into steam.

ex.main: **Warm, change, warm, change — heating alternates between raising the temperature and driving a phase change.** The two phase changes happen at fixed temperatures (0°C and 100°C for water) while the warming steps happen in between, which is the whole shape of a heating curve.
ex.tip: A phase change is a pause in the temperature, not a jump in it.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the six phase changes?
opts: Dissolving
Deposition
Sublimation
Condensation
questions.hint: A phase change moves between solid, liquid and gas. Which of these does something else?
steps: The six are melting, freezing, evaporation, condensation, sublimation and deposition.
Deposition, sublimation and condensation are all on that list.
Dissolving is sugar disappearing into water — two substances mixing, not one substance changing phase.
So dissolving is the odd one out.

ex.main: **Dissolving mixes two substances together; a phase change moves one substance between solid, liquid and gas.** Dissolved sugar has not melted — it is still sugar, spread through the water, and it can be recovered by evaporating the water away.
ex.tip: One substance changing, or two substances mixing? Different questions.

sorts.title: Does it take heat in, or give heat off?

items.t: An ice cube turning into a puddle
items.why: Melting — solid to liquid, up the ladder.

items.t: Water in a tray turning to ice in the freezer
items.why: Freezing — liquid to solid, down the ladder.

items.t: A puddle slowly disappearing on a warm day
items.why: Evaporation — liquid to gas, up the ladder.

items.t: Droplets forming on the outside of a cold can
items.why: Condensation — gas to liquid, down the ladder.

items.t: Dry ice smoking away without leaving a puddle
items.why: Sublimation — solid straight to gas, up the ladder.

items.t: Frost forming on a window overnight
items.why: Deposition — gas straight to solid, down the ladder.

items.t: A pot of water bubbling on a hot stove
items.why: Boiling — liquid to gas throughout, up the ladder.

items.t: Fog on a bathroom mirror after a shower
items.why: Condensation — the warm vapour becomes liquid on the cool glass.

items.t: A chocolate bar going soft in a warm pocket
Dew appearing on the grass before sunrise
items.why: Condensation — vapour in the air becomes liquid droplets.

items.t: Wet clothes drying on a line
items.why: Evaporation — the water leaves as a gas.
Freezing — liquid to solid. It does not have to be cold to count.
